notes:
Need to search first.I've written notes for most verses, but the coverage is uneven. My tools hit their usage limit early, so I could read only the parts of pages that showed up in search results. I never opened any page in full.

**Gaps:** I found nothing on vv. 12 ("hasten"), 13, 14 or 18 beyond Gill, and nothing on the "laid bare" vs. "burned up" wording question in v. 10. I also found no NET Bible notes, no Lutheran sources, no Catholic or Orthodox readings, and no material on prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace teaching. The StudyLight page I found for Wesley's Notes showed only Bible translations, not Wesley's own comments. Where I name a teacher's tradition and the page itself didn't say it, I mark it "(my label)" so you can check it.

---

**v. 1**
- Gill says this verse, read with 2 Peter 1:18, shows the writer is the Apostle Peter, who saw the Transfiguration. He calls them "beloved" because God chose them and gave them new birth. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_peter/3.htm
- Gill says a "pure mind" is not something people make for themselves. Only Christ's blood cleanses it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_peter/3.htm
- Gill says believers forget easily, so ministers need to keep reminding them. He sees this as proof that a regular preaching ministry is needed. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-peter-3.html

**v. 2**
- Gill says the "holy prophets" are the Old Testament prophets. They spoke about Christ's person, sufferings and coming glory, and the apostles taught nothing different. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_peter/3.htm
- Matthew Henry says what God spoke through the prophets and what Christ commanded through the apostles should be remembered often. Thinking about these things revives the believer. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Pe/2Pe_003.cfm
- Ligonier says Peter points readers to the prophets and apostles to show that false teaching was predicted. It does not take God by surprise. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/his-coming

**v. 3**
- Enduring Word (David Guzik) says scoffers should not surprise Christians. Their problem is moral, not just intellectual: they don't want Jesus as Lord of their lives. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-peter-3/
- Gill describes the scoffers as people who make light of sin, mock religion and ministers, and finally mock God himself. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-peter-3.html
- Calvin says the more God offers himself through the gospel, the bolder the ungodly become in their mockery. An editor's note on the CCEL page takes "last days" to mean the gospel age. https://www.ccel.org/study/2_Peter_3
- **Where readers differ on "last days":**
  - Most teachers take it as the whole time between Christ's first and second comings:
    - Ligonier, which bases this on Peter's use of Joel in Acts 2: https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/his-coming
    - The BibleHub study notes: https://biblehub.com/study/2_peter/3-3.htm
    - Guzik, who says the last days began at the Ascension: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-peter-3/
  - Constable's notes (on StudyLight) take it as the days just before Christ returns. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-peter/3-3.html
  - Gann's commentary (same page) is the minority view. It mentions the "whole Christian age" reading but thinks the phrase most likely means the last days of the Jewish nation, ending in AD 70. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-peter/3-3.html

**v. 4**
- Guzik says the scoffers assume things have always been as they are now and that God won't do anything new. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-peter-3/
- Ligonier says these were not honest questions. The false teachers were mocking the belief that Jesus will return as Judge. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/his-coming
- Gill says the scoffers don't name Christ, out of contempt. Their question means "What has become of the promise?" https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_peter/3.htm
- Calvin says the scoffers wrongly set the regular course of nature against God's promise. He compares them to people in his day with a little philosophy who chase ungodly speculation. https://www.ccel.org/study/2_Peter_3

**vv. 5–6**
- Guzik says the scoffers "willfully forget" creation and the Flood. He holds that believing literally in Creation, Adam and Eve, and Noah's Flood is essential. The earth has changed before, so God's promise to change it again shouldn't be mocked. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-peter-3/
- Gill (whom StudyLight labels a Calvinist Baptist) says the heavens were made from nothing by God's word, so they are not eternal and can be destroyed or changed. He explains "out of water and by water" with Genesis 1:2. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-peter/3-5.html
- Gill takes the Flood as worldwide, coming from above and below, after the world had stood 1,656 years. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_peter/3.htm

**v. 7**
- Gill says the same word that made heaven and earth now holds them up, "treasured up" for a final burning on Judgment Day. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_peter/3.htm

**v. 8**
- Guzik quotes Green: God sees time with a perspective we lack, since a thousand years may seem like a day. He also sees it with an intensity we lack, since one day can be like a thousand years. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-peter-3/
- Gill cites a Jewish source saying God puts off his anger with people so that they may repent. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_peter/3.htm

**v. 9 (the main point where Protestant traditions differ)**
- **Common ground:** Guzik says any delay is God's patience, giving people as much time as possible to repent. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-peter-3/
- **Ellicott** treats it as a practical answer: make good use of what looks to you like a delay. https://biblehub.com/2_peter/3-9.htm
- **Reformed and Calvinist reading:**
  - Ligonier says the verse is often used against predestination. But "you" means Peter's believing readers, so God doesn't want any of *them* to perish. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/lord-patient
  - John Samson on Monergism says "any" and "all" mean the elect. Read that way, he argues, the verse strongly supports election. https://www.monergism.com/blog/understanding-2-peter-39-john-samson-guest-post
  - Gill says "us-ward" is set apart from the scoffers and means the beloved. It is not true of every person. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_peter/3.htm
  - Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (on BibleHub) say God waits until the full number appointed to salvation is complete. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_peter/3-9.htm
  - Calvin (my label) takes a different line from the others. He says God's love for mankind is so great that he would have them all saved; the excerpt I saw breaks off there. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-peter/3-9.html
- **Arminian and Wesleyan reading:**
  - Adam Clarke (an early Methodist — my label) argues that since God wants no one to perish, he has never decreed anyone's damnation. Nor has he made salvation impossible for anyone, by forcing them to sin or by withholding the means of recovery. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-peter/3-9.html
  - Guzik quotes Clarke with approval. He adds that this is not a decree that no sinner will perish, but a picture of God's loving heart. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/archives/guzik_david/StudyGuide_2Pe/2Pe_3.cfm
  - Precept Austin says "any" points to individuals, not groups. It finds no hint of a secret decree sending some to damnation. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2_peter_39-10
- **Barnes (a middle view):** God sincerely wants everyone to be happy forever. But this describes what he wants now, not what he will do as Judge, so the verse does not teach that no one will perish. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_peter/3-9.htm
- Precept Austin also stresses that the verse does not teach universal salvation. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2_peter_39-10

**v. 10**
- Guzik says God's patient love can make it look as if Christ is delaying, but he will come, and at a time that surprises many. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-peter-3/
- Matthew Henry says a fire will go before the Lord and melt the elements. The earth, its people, and the works of nature and human skill will all be burned up and destroyed. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Pe/2Pe_003.cfm

**v. 11**
- Gill says believers should live with "loins girt" and lights burning, unlike the scoffers. They should keep watching, praying and reading, live soberly, and avoid worldliness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_peter/3.htm

**v. 13 (destroyed or renewed?)**
- Gill says the new heavens and earth will be new in quality, not in substance. They will be the present ones, purified by fire and cleansed of everything the curse brought. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_peter/3.htm
- Matthew Henry's wording on v. 10 is stronger ("destroyed"). But the part I saw doesn't take up the renewal question directly. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Pe/2Pe_003.cfm

**v. 14**
- Gill reads "found by him" as found "in him" (Philippians 3:9). Believers will stand at Christ's judgment wearing his righteousness, not their own. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_peter/3.htm

**v. 15**
- Gill says this patience is toward the elect. Toward the wicked it does not lead to salvation but to heavier punishment (Romans 2:4). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_peter/3.htm

**v. 16**
- Guzik quotes Clarke: the Greek word for "distort" means to rack or dislocate limbs. It describes people who force unnatural meanings onto God's word. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/archives/guzik_david/StudyGuide_2Pe/2Pe_3.cfm
- Matthew Henry says many people read Scripture without understanding it, or without being settled in it, and so are open to error. Twisting God's word leads to one's own ruin. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Pe/2Pe_003.cfm

**v. 17**
- Gill (Calvinist Baptist) says true saints "can never finally and totally fall." But they can lose their steadiness and start to doubt and waver. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-peter/3-17.html
- I didn't find an Arminian or Wesleyan comment on this verse to set beside Gill's.
- Matthew Henry says those led away by error become unsettled, like a wave tossed by the wind, so believers must keep watch. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Pe/2Pe_003.cfm
